Vide this judgment, I shall dispose of the aforementioned complaint case filed by the complainant, Sh. Ram Charan (hereinafter referred to as the Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:21:27 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 2 'complainant') against accused Mrs. Meena Bibi (hereinafter referred to as 'the accused'). 2. Factual Matrix: The complainant's case is that he is acquainted with the accused for last one year and the accused approached him for financial help citing that she requires money for her business, thus, on request of the accused, the complainant had given her loan of Rs.1,65,000/­ in cash on 08.03.2021 and regarding the same, the accused had also executed one hand written undertaking, as per which, the accused was supposed to return this amount within 2 months but the accused could not return the amount within 2 months and assured to make payment by June, 2021 and in discharge of the said liability, the accused issued the cheque in question bearing No. 652944 dated 29.06.2021 for a sum of Rs. 1,65,000/­ drawn on State Bank of India, Bera Champa Branch, Village Bera Champa, P.O. Devalaya, Dist. 24 Pargana North (West Bengal) 743424 (herein after referred to as the 'cheque in question') and when the said cheque was presented by the complainant, the same was dishonoured for the reason "insufficient funds" vide return memo dated 02.07.2021 and the return memo was received by the complainant on 16.07.2021. Thereafter, the complainant issued the legal demand notice dated 17.07.2021 U/S 138 of the N.I. Act , calling upon the accused to make the payment of the amount within 15 days and the same was duly served upon the accused. However, the accused neither filed reply to the same nor made any payment. Hence, being aggrieved, the complainant filed the present complaint under section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 on 24.08.2021 and prayed that the accused be summoned, tried and punished under section 138 of The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and be directed to pay fine equivalent to double the cheque amount and compensation be also granted to the complainant. 3. Summoning of accused: The court summoned the accused after Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:21:35 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 3 hearing the arguments at the stage of pre­summoning vide order dated 03.12.2021 and the accused entered appearance in the present case on 19.02.2022. 4. Notice: The court has framed notice of accusation under Section 251 Cr.P.C. against the accused on 26.05.2022. The substance of accusation was read over and explained to the accused and after being satisfied that the accused comprehended the same, the court recorded his plea. 5. Plea of the accused: The accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. She admitted her signatures on the cheque in question. She denied filling particulars of the cheque in question. She stated that she has not received the legal demand notice as her correct address is H. No. TA226, Gali No.2, Tuglakabad Extension, New Delhi where she is residing for last 11 years. In her defence, she stated that she had taken loan of Rs. 30,000/­ in three installments of Rs. 10,000/­ each from the complainant before Lockdown Period and thereafter, for 2 and 1/2 months, she went to her village at Village Dakshin Sherpur PO JADUR HATI, PS BADURIYA WEST BENGAL 743292 and when she returned from her village, the complainant took the cheque in question from her as security and the complainant told her that now she has liability for payment of Rs. 50,000/­ due to the interest accrued in the meantime. She stated that thereafter, in several installments on daily basis, she has returned the amount to the complainant, however, despite return of the amount, the complainant has misused the cheque in question. On the same date, the statement of accused was recorded U/S 294 Cr. P.C wherein he admitted correctness of dishonor memo pursuant to which the Bank witnesses mentioned at Sr. No. 2 record keeper / official from Complainant's Bank & Witness at Sr. No. 3 Record keeper / Clerk from accused's bank were dropped. 6. Evidence on behalf of complainant: To prove his case prima facie, the complainant has examined himself as CW­1 and has filed his evidence under Section Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:21:40 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. To support his case, the complainant has also placed on record Mark CW1/1(Colly) the original hand written note of the accused dt. 08.03.2021 regarding the payment made by the complainant to the accused, EX.CW1/2 original cheque in question dt. 29.06.2021, EX.CW1/3 the return memo dt. 02.07.2021, EX.CW1/4 the legal demand notice dt. 17.07.2021, along with it's postal receipts EX. CW1/5 and tracking report Mark CW1/6 and EX. CW1/7 the original complaint. Thereafter, CW­1 was subjected to cross examination. 7. He stated that the cheque in question was Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:21:44 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 5 given to him by accused in June, 2021 in presence of friends/relatives of accused and that the hand written note EX.CW1/1 was written by one person at instance of the accused. He denied the suggestion that he himself has written this note. He also denied the suggestion that he had obtained signature of Meena on this blank paper and later on wrote it's contents. He stated that he had given amount of Rs.1,65,000/­ to the accused returnable within 1­2 months. Examination of the accused under section 313 Cr.P.C: The accused was examined under section 313 Cr.P.C. on 29.08.2022, wherein she denied that she approached the complainant for financial help as she needed money for investment in her business and on her request, the complainant had given her loan of Rs.1,65,000/­ in cash on 08.03.2021. CW1/2. She stated that the loan amount was to be repaid in installments and she has already repaid the entire loan amount and she also has proof of the same. She also stated that the cheque in question was not given towards the Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:21:48 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 6 repayment of loan amount but as security at the time of advancement of loan. Evidence on behalf of Accused: In her defence, the Accused has examined herself as DW­1 wherein she adopted her statement recorded U/S 313 Cr. P.C as her examination­in­chief and also tendered copy of cash book maintained by the complainant i.e. EX. DW1/A (Colly 4 pages) (OSR). Thereafter, this witness was cross examined. During her cross examination, she stated that she cannot state as to what is written in circle A at page No.1 of EX. DW1/A (Colly) as she does not understand Hindi and she only understands Bengali. She denied the suggestion that as mentioned in page No. 1 of EX. DW1/A (colly), she had taken Rs.60,000/­ from the complainant. She stated that she had taken Rs. 35,000/­ from the complainant. She further stated that she cannot say whose name is written in Circle B at Page No.3 of EX. DW1/A (Colly) and stated that this card is of the complainant and his name and number is mentioned on the same. She denied the suggestion that as mentioned in Page No.3 of EX. DW1/A (Colly), she had taken Rs. 15,000/­ from the complainant in a separate transaction and she stated that the complainant had given her Rs. 35,000/­ in several instalments. She denied the suggestion that the transactions mentioned in EX. DW1/A (Colly) are different transactions than the transactions in question. She also denied the suggestion that the accused had given Rs. 1,65,000/­ to her on 08.03.2021 after withdrawing the same from his bank, as reflected in Bank Statement EX. CW1/8 (consisting of 2 pages) and stated that she was in her village at that point of time. She also denied the suggestion that she had Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:21:53 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 7 taken money from the complainant for business and stated that she does not do any business and she is working as Maid in one house of Mr. Shambhu in Gali No.3, at 3rd floor, RZ Block, Tughlakabad, and she does not know the house number. She denied the suggestion that she has kept 3­4 girls from Kolkata in her house who are doing the work of Prostitution. She denied the suggestion that the amount advanced by the complainant and the amount mentioned in the cards EX.DW1/A (Colly) are separate transactions. She denied the suggestion that she has not made any payment towards the cheque in question. She admitted that she had approached the complainant for availing money from him. She denied the suggestion that the complainant intimated her before presentation of the cheque in question. She denied the suggestion that after receiving the legal demand notice, she assured the complainant to make payment pursuant to their settlement. 10. Final Argument: Final arguments have been heard on behalf of the both the parties. The matter was then reserved for judgment. 11. In order to ascertain whether the accused has committed the offence under Section 138 of the NI Act, it is deemed fit to examine separately as to whether all the indispensable ingredients constituting the offence have been proved by the complainant. The offence under Section 138 of the NI Act has the following ingredients:­ a) Existence of legally enforceable debt or liability and issuance of cheque in discharge of said debt or liability; b) Dishonor of cheque in question which must have been drawn on an account drawn on an account maintained by the accused; c) Service of demand notice seeking payment of cheque amount within fifteen days from the date of service; d) Non­payment of cheque amount within fifteen days from the date of service of Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:21:58 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 8 notice; and e) Filing of complaint within one month from the date on which cause of action arises. 12. It is settled position of law that there is a presumption in favour of the complainant and against the accused. However, the presumption is rebuttable. The law as laid down in relation to the Negotiable Instruments Act is discussed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Rangappa v Sri Mohan (2010) 11 SCC 441 and the Hon'ble Supreme Court has held as under: "...15. In light of these extracts, we are in agreement with the respondent claimant that the presumption mandated by Section 139 of the Act does indeed include the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. To that extent, the impugned observations in Krishna Janardhan Bhat (supra) may not be correct. However, this does not in any way cast doubt on the correctness of the decision in that case since it was based on the specific facts and circumstances therein. As noted in the citations, this is of course in the nature of a rebuttable presumption and it is open to the accused to raise a defence wherein the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability can be contested. However, there can be no doubt that there is an initial presumption which favours the complainant. Section 139 of the Act is an example of a reverse onus clause that has been included in furtherance of the legislative objective of improving the credibility of negotiable instruments. While Section 138 of the Act specifies a strong criminal remedy in relation to the dishonour of cheques, the rebuttable presumption under Section 139 is a device to prevent undue delay in the course of litigation. However, it must be remembered that the offence made punishable by Section 138 can be better described as a regulatory offence since the bouncing of a cheque is largely in the nature of a civil wrong whose impact is usually confined to the private parties involved in commercial transactions. In such a scenario, the test of proportionality should guide the construction and interpretation of reverse onus clauses and the accused/defendant cannot be expected to discharge an unduly high standard or proof. In the absence of compelling justifications, reverse onus clauses usually impose an evidentiary burden Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:22:02 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 9 and not a persuasive burden..." 13. Keeping this in view, it is a settled position that when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of 'preponderance of probabilities'. Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. As clarified in the citations, the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. 14. Thus, it is settled that there is a presumption in favour of the complainant and against the accused, that the cheque was issued for consideration. However, the presumption is rebuttable. The accused can prove that the cheque was not issued for consideration or that the accused did not have any liability to pay the amount. For this, the accused need not lead evidence in support of his defence. He can prove it on the balance of probabilities by showing the contradictions in the material produced by the complainant. 15. In the present case, the accused has admitted her signatures and issuance of the cheque in question in favor of the complainant. It is also not in dispute admitted that the cheque is drawn on account of the accused. It is also admitted that the cheque was presented for encashment and that the same was dishonored for the reason "Funds Insufficient". However, the accused has denied the service of legal demand notice throughout the trial. It has been argued on behalf of the accused that there is no material on record to show that legal notice was served upon the accused. 16. Perusal of the record reveals that the legal demand notice dated 17.07.2021 Digitally signed AISHWARYA by AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:22:06 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 10 EX. CW1/4 was sent by the complainant at the address 'RZ 60B, Street No. 8/9, Kalkaji H.O. New Delhi­110019'. The same address is mentioned as the address of the accused in the memo of parties and in the agreement Mark CW1/1 (Colly). The claim of the accused is that the legal demand notice was not received by her as the same was sent at the wrong address as she is residing at 'H No. TA 226, Gali No.2, Tuglakabad Extension, New Delhi' for last 11 years. Despite such claim of the accused, the complainant has not lead any evidence to show that the accused was residing at RZ 60B, Street No. 8/9, Kalkaji H.O. New Delhi­110019, where he had sent the legal demand notice. Further, this claim of the accused is fortified by the documents filed by the complainant. The complainant has filed the copy of Aadhar Card of the accused along with hand written note Mark CW1/1 (Colly) upon which the complainant is relying to establish that he had extended loan of Rs. 1,65,000/­ to the accused on 08.03.2021. On this aadhar card, the address of the complainant is mentioned as H No. TA 226, Gali No.2, Tuglakabad Extension, Kalkaji, South Delhi 110019. Whereas, in hand written note Mark CW1/1, the address of the accused is mentioned as 'RZ 60B, Gali No. 8/9, Band Gali'. Admittedly, this hand written note Mark CW1/1 wherein the address of the accused is mentioned as RZ 60B, Gali No. 8/9, Band Gali, has not been written by the accused as the complainant during his cross examination stated that this was written by some other person at the instance of accused. The complainant has not offered any explanation as to why different address of the accused is mentioned in hand written note Mark CW1/1 than aadhar card of the accused and he has nowhere even mentioned the name of the person who has written the contents of hand written note and the accused has claimed that it's contents were written by the complainant himself. As such, it is established that the legal demand notice was sent at the wrong address of the accused. Now the question arises is as to whether a notice of demand sent on wrong address of the Drawer of the Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:22:11 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 11 cheque would amount to giving of notice to him/her as contemplated in Clause B of Proviso 2 of Section 138 of NI Act. Before determining this issue, it is necessary to discuss the legal position on this subject. Hon'ble Jammu & Kashmir High Court, in case titled as Engineering Controll v Banday Infratech Pvt. Ltd. , in CR.M.C NO. 381/2018 decided on 08.07.2022 has discussed this issue in detail, has held that: "... 10) Proviso to Section 138 of the NIA Act stipulates that three conditions must be satisfied before dishonourof a cheque can constitute an offence and become punishable. The first condition is that the cheque ought to have been presented before the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier. The second condition is that the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque must make a demand for payment of the amount of money by giving a notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding return of the cheque as unpaid. The third condition is that the drawer of such a cheque should have failed to make payment of the said amount of money to the payee or as the case may be to the holder in due course of the cheque within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. It is only upon the satisfaction of all the aforesaid three conditions that an offence under Section 138 can be said to have been committed by the person issuing the cheque. Thus, giving of notice of demand to the payee within the stipulated period after dishonor of a cheque is one of the necessary conditions for making out the offence under Section 138 of the NIA Act. 11) The Supreme Court in the case of D. Vinod Shivappa vs. Nanda Belliappa , (2006) 6 SCC 456, has elaborately dealt with a situation where the notice could not be served on the addressee for one or the other reason, such as his non availability at the time of delivery, or premises remaining locked on account of his having gone elsewhere etc. It was observed that if in each such case, the law is understood to mean that there has been no service of notice, it would completely defeat the very purpose of the Act. The Court further observed that it would then be very easy for an unscrupulous and dishonest drawer of a cheque to make himself scarce for sometime after issuing the cheque so that the requisite statutory notice can never be served upon him and consequently he can never be Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:22:16 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 12 prosecuted. The Court went on to observe that a person who can dodge the postman for about a month or two, or a person who can get a fake endorsement made regarding his non availability, can successfully avoid his prosecution because the payee is bound to issue a notice to him within a period of 30 days from the date of receipt of information from the bank regarding return of the cheque as unpaid. 12) The aforesaid observations were relied upon by the Supreme Court in the case of C. C. Alavi Haji (supra). However, it was observed by the Supreme Court that when the notice is sent by registered post by correctly addressing the drawer of the cheque, the mandatory requirement of issue of notice in terms of Clause (b) of proviso to Section 138 of the Act stands complied with. What the Supreme Court has emphasized is that the notice should have been sent on the correct address of drawer of the cheque. It is only then it can be said that notice has been received by the drawer of the cheque. 13) In Harman Electronics Private Limited and another v National Panasonic India Private Ltd , (2009) 1SCC 720, the Supreme Court has, while deliberating on the issue, observed as under: "13. It is one thing to say that sending of a notice is one of the ingredients for maintaining the complaint but it is another thing to say that dishonour of a cheque by itself constitutes an offence. For the purpose of proving its case that the accused had committed an offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the ingredients thereof are required to be proved. What would constitute an offence is stated in the main provision. The proviso appended thereto, however, imposes certain further conditions which are required to be fulfilled before cognizance of the offence can be taken. If the ingredients for constitution of the offence laid down in provisos (a),(b) and (c) appended to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are intended to be applied in favour of the accused, there cannot be any doubt that receipt of a notice would ultimately give rise to the cause of action for filing a complaint. As it is only on receipt of the notice that the accused at his own peril may refuse to pay the amount. Clauses (b) and (c) of the proviso to Section 138 therefore must be read together. Issuance of notice would not by itself give rise to a cause of action but communication of the notice would." 14) It was further observed by the Court that for constitution of an offence under Section 138 of the Act, the notice must be received by the accused. The Court went on to observe that it may be deemed to have been received in certain situations. An inference of having received the notice Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:22:21 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 13 by a drawer of a cheque can be raised only if the notice has been dispatched to his correct address. Such an inference cannot be drawn if the notice has been sent on the incorrect address of the drawer of the cheque..." 17. In the instant case, the aadhar card of the accused furnished by the complainant himself clearly shows that the address of the accused is not correctly mentioned in the notice of demand. Though the complainant has also mentioned another address of the accused in the memo of parties as "Village Dakshin Shedpur, P.O. Jadur Hati, PS Baduria, West Bengal­743292". However, the complainant has not filed any record to show that he had sent the legal demand notice at the said address as well. The complainant has only filed postal receipt and tracking report regarding the Delhi Address of the accused, thus, it can be safely concluded that the complainant has sent the legal demand notice at the incorrect address of the accused i.e. RZ 60B, Gali No. 8/9, Band Gali as the accused was residing at H No. TA 226, Gali No.2, Tuglakabad Extension, Kalkaji, South Delhi 110019. Once the material on record clearly suggests that the statutory notice of demand was sent by the complainant on a wrong address, the presumption of receipt of notice by the accused does not arise. Thus, the pre­condition of filing a complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act of sending a statutory notice has not been satisfied in the present case. Therefore, no cause of action arose in favour of the complainant to file the subject complaint. 18. Further, in the present case, Ld. Counsel for the accused has also argued that the accused did not fill other particulars of the cheque in question and therefore presumption must be drawn that the accused is not liable to make any payment and that the complainant had misused the cheque. I have considered the submission. I do not find any merits in it. It is no more res integra that the defence that particulars of Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:22:31 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 14 the cheque were not filled by the accused is no defence in a trial under Section 138 NI Act. The accused is liable for the offence under Section 138 NI Act, even if particulars of the cheque are not filled by the drawer of the cheque, if the liability of the drawer of the cheque / accused is proved as per law. Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Ravi Chopra v State And Anr. , 2008 SCC OnLine Del 351 has discussed in detail the issue related to the defence that there was no liability as cheque was given in blank. It has been held that even under the scheme of the NI Act it is possible for the drawer of a cheque to give a blank cheque signed by him to the payee and consent either implicitly or expressly to the said cheque being filled up at a subsequent point in time and presented for payment by the drawee. In the present case also, therefore, the defence taken by the accused that the cheque was blank is no defence to avoid the liability as the accused has admitted his signatures. 19. In this case, the accused has not disputed the factum of availing loan from the complainant, however, she has disputed the loan amount and the time of advancement of loan and she has further claimed that she has already repaid the entire amount, thus, she has claimed that her cheque in question which was given as security at the time of advancement of loan has been misused by the complainant as the same has not been returned despite repayment of loan amount. It has also been argued on behalf of accused that the complainant is running money lending business without any license, thus, it cannot be said that the cheque in question was issued in discharge of any legally enforceable debt or liability. Though, the complainant has denied running any money lending business, however, he has admitted that he had provided one card to the accused for receiving daily payment from the accused. The complainant has even given suggestion to the accused during cross examination with respect to card EX. DW1/A (Colly) that these cards are regarding separate transactions between the parties wherein once loan of Rs. 60,000/­ and at another Digitally signed by AISHWARYA AISHWARYA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2022.11.28 16:22:36 +0530 CC NI ACT No.6596 of 2021 Ram Charan Vs. Meena Page No. 15 time, loan of Rs. 15,000/­ was advanced by the complainant to the accused. Such suggestion of the complainant and admission of daily receipt of payment by the complainant from the accused vide cards EX. DW1/A (Colly), clearly establishes that the complainant was running money lending business. Now the question arises whether a complaint U/S 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act is maintainable even if the loan sanctioned by a professional money lender who does not have license as a professional money lender. On this point, it is relevant to refer to the observations made in J. Daniel v State of Kerala & Others , 2006 (1) Civil Court Cases 530 (Kerala) wherein it has been held that a dishonoured cheque which was issued for an unlawful consideration would not invoke the penal provisions of Section 138 NI Act. Explanation to Section 138 NI Act is pellucid in as much as 'debt or other liability' means a legally enforceable debt/liability. If any agreement is opposed to law or forbidden by law, it is not enforceable. If money is lent by a person without having the authority/license to do so, then it would be an unlawful agreement and consequently there would be no legally enforceable debt or liability. 20. For determination of this issue, it is also pertinent to refer to provisions of the Punjab Registration of Money Lender's Act, 1938 . Section 3 the Act, bars suits for recovery of a loan by a money lender not holding a valid licence. The point for consideration now is whether such a money lender, who does not have a valid money lending license, can successfully prosecute a person under provisions of the NI ACt. A bare perusal of the explanation to Section 138 NI Act would make it crystal clear that "debt or other liability" for the purposes of Section 138 means only a "legally enforceable debt or liability". The "debt" cannot be said to be "legally enforceable" when recovery of same has been barred by another law.
